content.title: Well-presented but with some flaws
content.review:
Summary:

The paper proposes two methods to reduce the number of parameters in the Transformer. The first one is on compressing the embedding layer, which stores the embedding matrix in low dimension and maps it to high dimension with a self-attention layer. The second one is to share all the Transformer layers except the first and the last layer. The model is tested on machine translation, language modeling, and summarization.

Reasons for score: 

The paper is well-written and the idea is clear. My concern is mainly on whether the contribution of this work is incremental. ~I’ll raise the score if the authors address the concerns below.~ Thanks for the additional experiments! I have raised my score to 6.



Pros: 

1. I like the finding that unsharing the first and the last layer can greatly improve the final performance of the model. This finding is valuable for people trying to compress the model with parameter sharing.
2. The authors test the model in a wide set of tasks and show consistent performance improvement.
3. The paper is clear and well-written and the idea is easy to understand.

Cons: 

1. For ablation studies in Table 2, the experiments are not fair for the baseline models because they have much fewer parameters. An ablation study with an equal number of parameters will be much stronger for the final result.
2. The first technique proposed by the paper is to increase the dimension of the compressed embedding vectors with self-attention. My main concern is this seems redundant to the first Transformer layer, where there is exactly a self-attention layer at the very beginning, and the only difference is the residual connection. This self-attention in the SAFE module becomes even more redundant given that you unshare the first Transformer layer. Some suggestions on experiments to resolve this issue:

    a. In experiments in Table 1, include a model with one extra layer for linear projection.

    b. In experiments in Table 3, include a model with only SAFE and a model with only Sandwich Module.

3. To compress the embedding matrix, how about directly reduce the vocabulary size? With BPE and subword vocabularies, this should be easy to achieve and can also significantly reduce the number of parameters in the embedding matrix.

Minor comments: 

- What exactly is “Every 2 layers shared” in Table 2? It would be better to define it clearly in the paper.
content.confidence: 5: The reviewer is absolutely certain that the evaluation is correct and very familiar with the relevant literature

content.title: Response to Reviewer 4
content.comment:
We thank the reviewer for their time and detailed feedback. We are happy to hear you find the findings valuable and writing clear, and understand your concerns. We respond to the points you make below and hope we address your concern and hope you will consider revising your assessment. 


**1\. For ablation studies in Table 2, the experiments are not fair for the baseline models because they have much fewer parameters. An ablation study with an equal number of parameters will be much stronger for the final result.**
We performed an experiment in which we increased the number of parameters in the *All-shared* (ALBERT-style) configuration to help strengthen our claim.  We increased the hidden dimension of the encoder and decoder layers to be $d_m = 768$ and $\vec{d}_m = 3072$, making the total parameter count 41M - slightly larger than our sandwich-style parameter sharing configuration (38M).  The final BLEU score on the test set is 21.95, indicating that the model doesn't perform well in this setting, even when scaling up.

**2\. Redundancy of SAFE embeddings**

The impact of self-attentive embeddings is that we are able to apply attention at a lower dimensionality, keeping parameter count down, while still achieving near-equivalent performance as directly using higher-dimensional embeddings. As shown in our experiments, we demonstrate its efficacy to this end. However, we understand your concerns which we address below:

Additional Experiments:
*2a. In experiments in Table 1, include a model with one extra layer for linear projection.*
We performed this experiment, adding an extra linear layer for the linear projection with dimension $d_e = 256$. Although the final result improves slightly, SAFE embeddings are empirically demonstrated to be effective. validating the usage of SAFE embeddings compared to other approaches.

| Model                                                          | Parameter Count | BLEU |  
|-|-|-|
| Linear, $d_e = 256$                                      | 53M                    | 27.1   |  
| Linear w/Additional Linear, $d_e=256$   | 54M                        | 27.2   |  
| SAFE, $d_e=256$                                          | 54M                       | 27.6  |  

*2b. In experiments in Table 3, include a model with only SAFE and a model with only Sandwich Module.*
In Table 1, there is a model with only SAFE at different sizes of $d_e$ - {128, 256}, while in Table 2 and 3 we have a model (denoted as Sandwich or Sandwich-base, respectively) which utilizes only Sandwich-style parameter sharing. It seems this was not particularly clear, so we will improve the presentation and include both results in Table 5. 

**3\. To compress the embedding matrix, how about directly reduce the vocabulary size?**
Thank you for pointing this out - it's an interesting point.  Although we agree this could be a potentially effective technique to decrease parameter count, the aim of our paper is to propose *architectural* changes to the Transformer architecture for more parameter efficiency instead of being too task-specific. We believe these techniques could be combined with our proposed architecture for increased parameter efficiency, and refer the reviewer to Kudo et al., 2018 and Sennrich et al., 2015.


**4. Meaning of Every 2 Layers Shared**
Every 2 layers shared indicates a weight sharing technique in which we share every 2 layers for both the (6-layer) encoder and the decoder. We will take your advice and define this more clearly in the paper.

We once again thank the reviewer for their feedback and hope that our response alleviates their concerns.

*We will add (edit: We have added) these results in an updated version of the paper

---

[1]: Kudo, Taku, and John Richardson. "Sentencepiece: A simple and language-independent subword tokenizer and detokenizer for neural text processing." arXiv preprint arXiv:1808.06226 (2018).

[2]: Sennrich, Rico, Barry Haddow, and Alexandra Birch. "Neural machine translation of rare words with subword units." arXiv preprint arXiv:1508.07909 (2015).

display_title: weak baselines and lacking empirical evidence

content.title: weak baselines and lacking empirical evidence
content.review:
The paper studies parameter reduction approaches for encoder-decoder transformer models that are used in sequence-to-sequence tasks.  The parameter reduction approaches proposed are similar to those presented in the ALBERT model proposed by Lan et al., but there are differences such as adding a self-attention transformer layer with embedding factorization, and empirical determination of which layers can share parameters and which layers need to remain untied to achieve best performance on sequence-to-sequence tasks.

Two main contributions of the paper in my view are:
a) The Self-attentive factorized embeddings which are shown to perform better than the embedding factorization proposed by Lan et al.
b) The results of table 2 that show that sharing all layers of encoder (as done in the ALBERT model) as well as sharing all layers of the decoder model leads to very poor performance on seq-to-seq tasks.

However, when demonstrating the value of the proposed sandwich style parameter sharing approach I feel the empirical results are very unclear and fall short of being convincing.  For instance, it is not clear how the various baselines are selected and certain others are left out.  For instance
a) On the WMT’14 EN-DE task the Evolved Transformer w/ 48M parameters is BLEU of 27.7 but the 64.1M parameter model has BLEU of 28.4.  Only the 48M parameter result is mentioned.  Among the bigger models, the Evolved Transformer deep model has 218M parameters and achieves BLEU score of 29.5.  What is the reason for leaving this out?
b) On the Wikitext-103 LM task, the kNN-LM approach of Khandelwal et al. achieves, with 247M parameters, a perplexity of 15.79 which is 25% relative better than the subformer ppl of 20.39 reported in the paper.  Similarly there are Transformer XL models with 257M parameters which obtain PPL of 16.4 (Krause et al.).  Why are these, and other beselines which are between PPL of 15-20 (and this is a huge range!) and many of them are transformer based, not mentioned?
c) Similarly, on the CNN-daily mail summarization task, there are models w/ Rouge-1 of over 44, and quite a few models in the 41-44 range which perform better than the proposed model performance of Rouge-1 of 40.9.
content.rating: 4: Ok but not good enough - rejection

content.title: Response to Reviewer 1
content.comment:
We thank the reviewer for their time and feedback. We are confident that after clarifying the points highlighted by the reviewer, we can resolve any ambiguities that hinder the message and potential impact of the paper. It would be extremely valuable if we could hear your thoughts on our response so we can make appropriate modifications to the paper.

Regarding the comments with respect to the baselines to compare with our model, we would like to point out that our main goal is not to outperform every specialized task-specific Transformer model in the literature of a given task, but rather improve on the original Transformer architecture and its parameter-efficient variants for the tasks at hand. With this in mind, we feel that the comparisons on the language modeling/summarization benchmark you mention would be unfair as they (1) are much larger than the comparisons we make (~2.5x larger) and (2) often focus on modifying the core attention mechanism or using specialized training techniques such dynamic evaluation (such as that found in Krause et al., 2019) - something we do not tackle in this paper. 

However, we do agree that the experiment with the Evolved Transformer to be useful for a fairer comparison - we will run an experiment to more directly compare with this and update the paper with the results.

We hope that our response clarifies your concerns and that you will consider revising your evaluation as a result.

Thank you  

---

content.title: Response
content.comment:
Though we understand where the reviewer is coming from, given that So et al., 2019 controlled for this difference with their GPU experiments and that we have also run experiments on GPUs, our model outperforms the Evolved Transformer baseline when the hardware is controlled for. Furthermore, given that the usage of TPUs results in this significant of a difference, it is all the more necessary to control for this variable.

When calculating the standard deviation (averaged over 5 runs) we find the results of our Subformer configuration to be $28.5 \pm 0.06$ - indicating that the results are statistically significant compared to the Evolved Transformer which reports $28.2 \pm 0.1$. 

Moreover, the result of 27.7 for Transformer-base is a widely reported result when reimplemented by various papers (Ghazvininejad et al., 2019, Kasai et al., 2020, Mehta et al., 2020), with even So et al., 2019 reporting the same result - tested for significance - when running Transformer-base on a GPU. In contrast, when the exact same model is run on TPUs, So et al., 2019 reports a BLEU score of 28.2, further reinforcing this point.

We hope this helps alleviate the reviewer's concerns.

content.title: Very weak paper
content.review:
This paper proposes Subformer, a variant of efficient Transformers that aims to reduce parameters by parameter sharing or sandwich based parameter sharing.  I think this is overall a very weak submission probably at best, only good for a student workshop at maybe a NLP conference. 

The authors proposed SAFE which stands for self-attentive factorized embeddings. This section is poorly described that that it is confusing. In fact, being very well acquainted with Transformers and their variants even in this line of work, I had troubles understanding what the authors are doing. The naming factorized is strange because there is actually no factorization happening. At best, this is just adding another smaller projection layer to that layer. Am I missing something here? Nevertheless, the writing can be significantly improved.

The next "contribution" is the sandwich layers and shared parameters of sandwich layers. This is an ad-hoc scheme that might not be a strong contribution for a conference paper.

Experiments section are not fantastic, but also not very convincing. In fact, at approximately the *same* parameter costs, this method does almost exactly the same as the baselines (!!) on MT. On the other datasets, there is also insufficient experiments or ablations to show a parameter-by-parameter apples to apples comparison. 

In terms of constructive feedback, I would personally hope to see more controlled experiments and even more comparisons with other weight sharing schemes presented in Albert or other models. It is also worth considering pretraining experiments like in Albert or Electra. There is nothing much that one can do to the idea, so im just hoping the authors can improve the experiments and perhaps resubmit it to a workshop in the future. With a stronger set of empirical results I think this paper will stand a better chance in the future.

content.title: Response to Reviewer 5
content.comment:
We thank the anonymous reviewer for the feedback, but respectfully disagree regarding many of the points raised in the review, namely:

1. lack of understanding of certain points
2. the usage of the word **factorization** in the naming
3. the parameter costs almost the same on MT as baseline
4. insufficient experiments, lack of novelty - and *no improvements at all*

We respond to the points you make below and hope that through our discussion we can make appropriate adjustments to the paper to satisfy you that the work in question at least contributes enough to warrant publication, and that you will consider revising your assessment. 

---
1. Lack of understanding at certain points   
We understand that the reviewer has concerns about the state of the paper, however given the current review, and its lack of specific feedback, we are not entirely clear about a path for improvement. We would appreciate if the reviewer could provide more details and point out more specifically what could be improved. We would be grateful for this useful input.

2. Usage of the word **factorization**:    
According to the definition of factorization (from Wikipedia), "...factorization or factoring consists of writing a number or another mathematical object as a product of several factors, usually smaller or simpler objects of the same kind." Given this, as our SAFE embeddings represents the token embeddings as an operation on lower dimensional, smaller vectors, we believe the usage of the word *factorization* in the naming to be correct. Also, we would like the reviewer to take note that Lan et al., 2020 also used the term "factorized" to refer to their technique using a linear projection.

3. ...the parameter costs almost the same on MT as baseline    
For the sake of providing a complete picture, we compare with DeLighT (Mehta et al., 2020) - the baseline that the anonymous reviewer mentions. However, we are sure to note that this work is **contemporaneous** (also submitted to ICLR 2021 https://openreview.net/forum?id=ujmgfuxSLrO) - and provides an improvement in terms of both overall performance and per-parameter performance. Additionally, we outperform the baseline on the language modeling task by a considerable margin, while using the same number of parameters. For these reasons, we believe that this complaint is inadequately supported.

4. Insufficient Experiments, results do not represent any improvement at all    
As our aim is to improve on the original Transformer architecture on sequence generation tasks, we believe that we have experimented on multiple benchmarks - providing empirical evidence to support our hypothesis. However, if the reviewer believes that the experiments are insufficient despite this, we would be grateful if the reviewer could point out specific examples to improve the paper. We believe the pretraining experiments suggested are orthogonal to the direction of the paper, given that we argue for architectural improvements for *sequence generation tasks*.

---

[1]: Lan, Zhenzhong, Mingda Chen, Sebastian Goodman, Kevin Gimpel, Piyush Sharma, and Radu Soricut. "Albert: A lite bert for self-supervised learning of language representations." *International Conference on Learning Representations 2020*

[2]: Mehta, Sachin, Marjan Ghazvininejad, Srinivasan Iyer, Luke Zettlemoyer, and Hannaneh Hajishirzi. "DeLighT: Very Deep and Light-weight Transformer." arXiv preprint arXiv:2008.00623 (2020).

content.title: Response
content.comment:
Hi, I have read your rebuttal and also other reviewer's comments and concerns.

My score remains unchanged because I still feel the rebuttal does not address the core concerns of this work. 

The main problem here with the experiment results are as follows:

1) While it is true that DeLight was concurrent work and there was no need to compare with it, there is no Transformer baseline in a comparable, ablative setup as Subformer on the LM task. So I would suggest getting this apples-to-apples comparison. 

2) For summarization, you should compare with a Transformer with *equal* parameters as Subformer. How do we not know that a smaller Transformer will perform just as well as Subformer. A diagram sweeping the compute-performance trade-off of Transformer vs Subformer will ease concerns. Compute here refers to both memory and inference speed.

I think the empirical comparisons are not conclusive. DeLight was published on Arxiv on 3rd Aug (one day after the contemporaneous period), I agree that you are not required to compare with it. But then you would not have any lightweight baseline left to compare against. Not to mention on LM, aside from Transformer-XL (which is obviously a very different setup), there is no comparison of a Transformer on your setup. This is also the same for summarization. These are things that can be fixed to make the paper stronger. So I suggest actually comparing with something like Albert or other models that do weight sharing. 

If you really wanted to make your case, I would suggest making a performance-compute trade-off at several parameter sizes and compare subformer, transformer and something like Albert. If the performance-compute trade-off chart looks good, I will raise my score.

content.title: Response to Reviewer 5's Response
content.comment:
We thank the reviewer for their comments, which we address below:

**1\. While it is true that DeLight was concurrent work and there was no need to compare with it, there is no Transformer baseline in a comparable, ablative setup as Subformer on the LM task. So I would suggest getting this apples-to-apples comparison.**

Following the reviewer's advice, we performed this experiment, using adaptive input embeddings and a comparable, ablative setup as the Subformer (shown below):  

| Model | Parameter Count | Perplexity |
|-|-|-|
| Transformer (4 Layer) | 96M | 26.42 |
| Transformer (8 Layer) | 146M | 22.32 |
| Subformer | 96M | **20.39**| 

As can be seen, even when performing experiments in a similar setup, we can see that the Subformer vastly outperforms both models, demonstrating evidence for efficiency and performance of the Subformer when compared to Transformer variants in an apples to apples comparison.

**2\. For summarization, you should compare with a Transformer with equal parameters as Subformer. How do we not know that a smaller Transformer will perform just as well as Subformer.**

To address the reviewers concern about the possibility of a smaller Transformer outperforming a larger sized model on this task, we performed this experiment, using the same parameters as the Subformer by reducing the number of layers from 6 $\rightarrow$ 3. The results for this experiment can be seen below:

| Model | Parameter Count | R1 | R2 | RL |
|-|-|-|-|-|
| Transformer (3 Layer) | 57M | 40.0 | 17.5 | 36.7  |
| Transformer-base (Edunov et al., 2019) | 77M | 40.1 |  17.6 | 36.8 |
| Subformer | 57M | **40.9** | **18.3** | **37.7**


From this experiment, it is empirically shown that the Subformer outperforms both Transformer configurations. We also take note of the fact that using a smaller Transformer underperforms the larger Transformer for this task. 

**3\. Performance-Compute Trade-Off**  
In addition to the above the results, heeding the reviewer's advice, we will develop a diagram with a sweep of the compute-performance trade-off, and add it to an updated version of the paper. We will add a comment on this once the diagrams are ready.

We thank the reviewer for their detailed comments and thank them for making the paper stronger as a result.

replying_to: Replying to Response to Reviewer 5's Response

content.title: About your smaller Transformer
content.comment:
Thanks for conducting the extra experiments.

I would like to point out: when you reduce the params to make them comparable, it doesn't seem appropriate to simply shrink the number of layers.  By this logic, if I want to reduce a 4-layer Transformer by something like 4x, I would simply reduce it to one layer. This is no longer about representation capability but changes the inductive biases too drastically (this is just an illustrative example and not exactly to scale and I understand that there are params that are not in the transformer blocks).  The more correct is to scale the FFN or hidden size of the model to correctly scale the Transformer down.
